cards.back: Level I: full subspecialty coverage 24/7 with research and residency. Level II: 24/7 surgery, most subspecialties, no research requirement. Level III: emergency surgery and stabilization, transfers out. Level IV: stabilization and transfer.

cards.front: What are the physiologic field triage criteria?
cards.back: GCS of 13 or less, systolic blood pressure under 90, or respiratory rate under 10 or over 29. Any one sends the patient to the highest level of trauma care available.

cards.front: How do you transport a pregnant trauma patient past 20 weeks, and why?
cards.back: Tilted 15 to 30 degrees to the left, or with the board wedged, to keep the uterus off the vena cava. Blood volume rises 40 to 50 percent, so she hides blood loss well.

quiz.q: Which fall height is considered a significant mechanism of injury in an adult?
choices: Greater than 6 feet
Greater than 10 feet
Greater than 20 feet
Greater than 30 feet
quiz.why: The adult threshold is greater than 20 feet, roughly two stories. Ten feet is the pediatric threshold, along with 2 to 3 times the child's height. Six feet is a standing fall and 30 feet is higher than the guideline requires.

quiz.q: A driver struck a tree at highway speed. The windshield is starred, the steering wheel is bent, and he says only that his neck is sore. What does the scene tell you?
choices: The chest and head absorbed major energy, so suspect injuries he is not reporting
The airbag protected him because it deployed
A sore neck with no other complaint rules out serious injury
The windshield damage came from debris, not the patient
quiz.why: A starred windshield and a deformed steering wheel are second-collision evidence of head and chest impact. Airbags deflate in about 0.05 seconds and do not prevent all injury, and a single complaint never rules out the silent third collision inside the organs.

quiz.q: A patient was shot once in the abdomen with a handgun. He has one small wound and no exit wound. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: A single small wound means minimal internal damage
Absence of an exit wound means the bullet lost most of its energy harmlessly
Only the organs directly under the wound can be injured
The bullet's path is unknown and internal injury may be extensive
quiz.why: A bullet tumbles, ricochets off bone, and delivers energy off its visible path, so a small hole tells you nothing about the track. No exit wound actually means all of the projectile's energy stayed inside the patient.

quiz.q: How far above a wound should a tourniquet be placed?
choices: Directly over the wound
2 to 3 inches above the wound, never over a joint
At the most distal point of the limb
As close to the armpit or groin as physically possible in every case
quiz.why: Two to three inches proximal captures the artery without crushing the wound itself, and joints have no compressible soft tissue so a tourniquet over one will not occlude flow. High-and-tight placement is a combat variation, not the default civilian teaching.

quiz.q: A patient has a partial amputation of the left forearm with pulsatile bright red bleeding soaking the carpet. What is your first action?
choices: Apply a pressure dressing and elevate the arm
Hold direct pressure for 3 minutes and reassess
Apply a tourniquet to the upper arm and note the time
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze
quiz.why: Amputations and spurting arterial bleeds go straight to a tourniquet rather than climbing the ladder. Elevation is no longer used, direct pressure wastes time on an arterial amputation, and packing is for junctional wounds you cannot tourniquet.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after you apply a tourniquet, the patient begs you to loosen it because of the pain. What should you do?
choices: Leave it in place, explain that the pain is expected, and transport
Loosen it briefly to let blood return, then retighten
Remove it and switch to a pressure dressing
Loosen it just until a faint distal pulse returns
quiz.why: A tourniquet is never loosened in the field. Releasing it restarts the bleeding, washes out the clot, and can send acid and potassium from the ischemic limb into circulation. Pain is expected and is not a reason to release.

quiz.q: A patient has a deep laceration high in the right groin with heavy dark and bright bleeding. Direct pressure with a bulky dressing has not controlled it. What is the best next step?
choices: Apply a tourniquet as high on the thigh as possible
Add more dressings and continue direct pressure for another 5 minutes
Elevate the leg and apply pressure at the femoral pressure point
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze and hold firm pressure for 3 minutes
quiz.why: The groin is a junctional site where a tourniquet has nothing to compress against, so packing is the tool. Piling on dressings without reaching the vessel does nothing, and elevation and pressure points have been removed from bleeding control.

quiz.q: Approximately how much blood volume must an adult lose before the systolic blood pressure begins to fall?
choices: About 10 percent
About 30 percent
About 50 percent
About 5 percent
quiz.why: Vasoconstriction and tachycardia defend the pressure until roughly 30 percent, about 1500 mL, is gone, which is the class II to class III boundary. That is exactly why a normal blood pressure is not reassurance in trauma.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old man from a motorcycle crash is anxious, pale, and cool with a heart rate of 132, blood pressure 104/88, and capillary refill of 4 seconds. What best describes his condition?
choices: He is stable because his blood pressure is normal
He has neurogenic shock from a spinal injury
He is in compensated hemorrhagic shock and needs rapid transport
He is having an anxiety reaction to the crash
quiz.why: Tachycardia, cool pale skin, a narrowed pulse pressure, and delayed capillary refill with a maintained systolic is textbook compensated shock. Neurogenic shock gives warm dry skin with bradycardia, and calling it anxiety ignores every perfusion finding.

quiz.q: That same patient becomes calm and stops complaining, and his blood pressure is now 78/50 with a heart rate of 146. What has happened?
choices: He is improving because his anxiety has resolved
His pain has been controlled by endorphins
He is entering decompensated shock as compensation fails
The first blood pressure reading was inaccurate
quiz.why: A quiet patient with a falling pressure and rising heart rate is failing, not improving. Compensation is adrenaline-funded and runs out abruptly, and deteriorating mental status is a perfusion sign. Assuming a bad first reading ignores the trend in every other vital.

quiz.q: Which intervention most directly addresses the coagulopathy of a bleeding trauma patient at the EMT level?
choices: Administering high-flow oxygen
Raising the patient's legs
Giving oral fluids for volume
Removing wet clothing and keeping the patient warm
quiz.why: Clotting enzymes slow sharply as core temperature falls, so preventing hypothermia directly protects clot formation. Oxygen treats hypoxia rather than clotting, leg elevation has no proven benefit in trauma, and nothing by mouth is the rule for a likely surgical patient.

quiz.q: Which Glasgow Coma Scale motor score corresponds to a patient who purposefully reaches toward the site where you apply a painful stimulus?
quiz.why: Reaching toward the stimulus is localizing, which scores 5. Six requires following a verbal command, 4 is simply pulling the limb away, and 3 is abnormal flexion or decorticate posturing.

quiz.q: A boxer is knocked out for 30 seconds, wakes up and chats normally for 20 minutes, then becomes rapidly unresponsive with a dilated left pupil. Which injury does this pattern describe?
choices: Concussion
Subdural hematoma
Epidural hematoma
Diffuse axonal injury
quiz.why: A lucid interval followed by rapid decline is the classic epidural hematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery. A subdural bleeds slowly from veins over days, a concussion does not produce a blown pupil, and diffuse axonal injury does not have a lucid interval.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient has clear fluid draining from his right ear. What should you do?
choices: Cover it loosely with a sterile dressing and allow it to drain
Pack the ear canal with sterile gauze to stop the flow
Irrigate the canal with saline
Insert an occlusive dressing to prevent infection
quiz.why: Clear drainage suggests cerebrospinal fluid from a basilar skull fracture. Packing or occluding the canal raises intracranial pressure and traps infection inside, and irrigation pushes contamination toward the brain.

quiz.q: An intubated head-injury patient being bagged at 12 per minute develops a blood pressure of 200/90, pulse 44, a fixed dilated right pupil, and extensor posturing. What is the appropriate change?
choices: Slow ventilations to 8 per minute to reduce airway pressure
Continue at 12 per minute and transport
Lower the head of the bed below the level of the heart
Increase ventilations to 20 per minute while the herniation signs persist
quiz.why: These are active herniation signs, the only indication for controlled hyperventilation at 20 per minute, which briefly reduces intracranial pressure. Slowing ventilation raises carbon dioxide and worsens swelling, and head-down positioning increases intracranial pressure further.

quiz.q: Which finding is characteristic of neurogenic shock rather than hemorrhagic shock?
choices: Cool, pale, diaphoretic skin
Warm, dry skin with bradycardia
Rapid thready pulse with delayed capillary refill
Narrowed pulse pressure with intense thirst
quiz.why: Loss of sympathetic tone dilates vessels and blocks the compensatory tachycardia, so the patient is hypotensive with warm dry skin and a slow or normal heart rate. Every other choice describes the adrenaline-driven picture of hemorrhagic shock.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old rolled his car. He is alert and oriented, denies neck or back pain, has no midline tenderness, moves everything, is not intoxicated, and has an obviously deformed and painful right femur. What spinal care applies?
choices: No restriction, since he denies spinal pain
Collar only and let him walk to the stretcher
Apply spinal motion restriction because the femur is a distracting injury
Full long board with head blocks and straps for transport
quiz.why: A painful femur is a distracting injury, so he fails selective clearance no matter how his neck feels, and restriction is indicated. Modern restriction means a collar with a scoop or vacuum device onto the stretcher, not a rigid long board for the whole transport.

quiz.q: Which statement about long backboards reflects current practice?
choices: The board is an extrication and transfer device, not a transport device
Every patient with a significant mechanism must be boarded
Boards reduce pressure injuries compared with a padded stretcher
Boarding improves neurologic outcomes in penetrating neck trauma
quiz.why: Long boards cause pressure injury and restrict breathing with no demonstrated outcome benefit, so they are used to move a patient and then removed. Boarding penetrating trauma actively harms by delaying surgery, and mechanism alone no longer mandates restriction.

quiz.q: An unresponsive motorcyclist is breathing 6 times per minute with a full-face helmet in place. What is correct?
choices: Leave the helmet on and ventilate through the face shield
Leave the helmet on and transport immediately
Remove the helmet after arrival at the hospital
Remove the helmet with two providers maintaining in-line stabilization so you can ventilate
quiz.why: Inadequate ventilation is an absolute indication for helmet removal, done by two providers with one stabilizing the jaw and occiput from below. You cannot deliver an effective mask seal through a face shield, and delaying until the hospital leaves the patient hypoxic.

quiz.q: How many sides of an occlusive dressing over an open chest wound should be taped down if a commercial vented seal is unavailable?
choices: All four
Three
Two
None; leave the dressing loose
quiz.why: Taping three sides creates a one-way flutter valve: air cannot enter through the hole but can escape on exhalation. Four sides can trap air and cause a tension pneumothorax, while a loose or two-sided dressing does not seal the wound during inhalation.

quiz.q: A stabbing victim suddenly becomes severely short of breath with a blood pressure of 76/40, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the most likely problem?
choices: Cardiac tamponade
Hemothorax on the right
Tension pneumothorax on the right
Simple pneumothorax
quiz.why: Absent unilateral breath sounds with JVD and hypotension is a tension pneumothorax; tracheal deviation is late and may never appear. Tamponade leaves breath sounds equal, hemothorax gives flat neck veins and dull percussion, and a simple pneumothorax does not drop the pressure.

quiz.q: An elderly man struck the steering wheel and has a segment of the left chest that pulls inward when he inhales. What is the most appropriate management?
choices: Positive-pressure ventilation with a bag-valve-mask
Tape a bulky dressing over the segment to stop the motion
Place a sandbag on the segment and secure it
Have him lie on the uninjured side to splint the chest
quiz.why: Positive-pressure ventilation splints the flail segment from the inside and treats the pulmonary contusion underneath, which is the real killer. Taping or sandbagging restricts chest expansion and worsens ventilation, and positioning alone does not address the contusion.

quiz.q: A patient with a sealed chest wound deteriorates in the ambulance: rising anxiety, pressure falling from 118 to 84 systolic, and breath sounds now absent on the injured side. ALS is 10 minutes away. What do you do first?
choices: Begin chest compressions
Replace the seal with a tighter fully occlusive dressing
Increase the oxygen flow rate and continue to the hospital
Lift a corner of the seal to release trapped air, then reassess
quiz.why: You have most likely converted the open pneumothorax into a tension, and burping the seal is the immediate, reversible fix available to an EMT. Making the seal tighter worsens it, oxygen alone does not relieve trapped pressure, and the patient still has a pulse.

quiz.q: Which organ group bleeds heavily when injured rather than spilling its contents?
choices: Stomach and small bowel
Liver, spleen, and kidneys
Gallbladder and bladder
Large intestine and appendix
quiz.why: Liver, spleen, kidneys, and pancreas are solid, vascular organs that hemorrhage. Stomach, bowel, gallbladder, and bladder are hollow and spill contents, producing peritonitis over hours rather than immediate blood loss.

quiz.q: A restrained driver has a bruise across the lower abdomen, mild tenderness, and normal vital signs. What is the correct disposition?
choices: Refusal is reasonable because the vitals are normal
Transport only if the pain worsens over the next hour
Transport for evaluation because a seat-belt sign predicts internal injury
Apply ice and advise follow-up with a primary care provider
quiz.why: A seat-belt sign markedly raises the probability of bowel, mesenteric, and lumbar spine injury, and hollow-organ injuries declare themselves over hours. Normal vitals early mean nothing, and waiting on scene or at home wastes the window before peritonitis sets in.

quiz.q: A worker has a screwdriver impaled in the left cheek with bleeding into the mouth that he is choking on. What should you do?
choices: Remove the object and control bleeding from both sides of the cheek
Stabilize it in place with bulky dressings and suction around it
Push the object through to the outside of the cheek
Place the patient supine and stabilize the object
quiz.why: The cheek is the one anatomic exception where an impaled object is removed, because it cannot be stabilized without threatening the airway and bleeding drains into the mouth. Leaving it in place with an airway already compromised risks aspiration, and supine positioning makes that worse.

quiz.q: Before and after applying any splint, what must be assessed and documented?
choices: Blood pressure in both arms
Pupil size and reactivity
Lung sounds in all fields
Distal circulation, motor function, and sensation
quiz.why: CMS confirms that the splint did not compromise the limb and documents a baseline if the limb worsens later. Blood pressure, pupils, and lung sounds are part of the overall assessment but say nothing about whether the splint is choking the extremity.

quiz.q: A patient fell from a roof and has pelvic pain, a heart rate of 128, and a blood pressure of 88/60. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
choices: Apply a traction splint to both legs
Apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters and transport rapidly
Rock the pelvis to confirm instability before binding
Log roll the patient repeatedly to inspect the back and buttocks
quiz.why: An unstable pelvis can hold 2 liters of blood, and closing the ring with a binder over the greater trochanters reduces that space. Rocking the pelvis and repeated rolling break clot, and traction splints are contraindicated when the pelvis is fractured.

quiz.q: A cyclist has an isolated closed deformity of the mid-thigh with a strong pedal pulse, no pelvic tenderness, and no knee injury. Which device is indicated?
choices: Long board with the legs strapped together
Vacuum splint only
Traction splint
Sling and swathe
quiz.why: An isolated closed mid-shaft femur fracture is the sole indication for a traction splint, which reduces the thigh compartment volume and pain. A long board does not realign the femur, a vacuum splint alone provides no traction, and sling and swathe is for the upper extremity.

quiz.q: A patient whose forearm was splinted 15 minutes ago now reports severe burning and numbness in the fingers, which are pale and cool. What is the best action?
choices: Loosen the splint, recheck circulation, motor, and sensation, and reassess
Leave the splint alone since removing it may displace the fracture
Elevate the arm above the head to reduce swelling
Apply an ice pack over the splint to control swelling
quiz.why: New pallor, coolness, and numbness distal to a splint means the splint or swelling is compressing circulation, and loosening it is both the diagnosis and the treatment. Leaving it risks limb loss, and elevation above heart level lowers perfusion pressure further.

quiz.q: Using the adult rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area does one entire leg represent?
choices: 9 percent
13.5 percent
14 percent
18 percent
quiz.why: Each adult leg is 18 percent, front and back combined. Nine percent is an arm or the head, and 13.5 percent is the pediatric value for a leg in an infant, where the head takes a larger share.

quiz.q: A man spilled a dry industrial powder on his forearm and it is burning. What is the correct first step?
choices: Flush immediately with copious water for 20 minutes
Brush the dry powder off, then flush with copious water for 20 minutes
Neutralize the chemical with a weak base before flushing
Apply a dry sterile dressing and transport without flushing
quiz.why: Water activates dry agents such as lime, so the powder is brushed off first and then the site is flushed for at least 20 minutes. Neutralizing generates heat and a second burn, and a dressing over active chemical leaves it burning.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has circumferential partial thickness burns around the entire right forearm from a grease fire. Why is this considered a critical burn?
choices: Circumferential burns always involve full thickness tissue
Grease burns are chemical rather than thermal
Swelling within a circumferential burn can cut off circulation like a tourniquet
Circumferential burns count double in the rule of nines
quiz.why: Burned tissue swells and a rigid circumferential eschar cannot expand, so pressure rises until it occludes blood flow distally. Circumferential burns are critical regardless of depth, grease is a thermal agent, and surface area is counted normally.

quiz.q: Firefighters hand you a man from a basement fire who is confused, with a headache, nausea, soot around his mouth, and an SpO2 of 100 percent. Your partner says his oxygenation is fine. What is the correct response?
choices: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 lpm because the oximeter cannot detect carbon monoxide
Withhold oxygen since the saturation is 100 percent
Apply a nasal cannula at 2 lpm for comfort
Treat the confusion as a head injury and restrict spinal motion
quiz.why: Carboxyhemoglobin is read by the pulse oximeter as though it were oxyhemoglobin, so a perfect reading in a fire victim is meaningless. High-flow oxygen shortens carbon monoxide's half-life dramatically, and a low-flow cannula will not do it.

quiz.q: Which patient meets an anatomic field triage criterion for the highest level of trauma care available?
choices: A 62-year-old who fell from standing and has hip pain
A driver whose airbag deployed with no complaints
A patient with an isolated closed forearm fracture
A patient with a flail chest after a side impact crash
quiz.why: Flail chest is on the anatomic criteria list along with penetrating torso injury, two proximal long bone fractures, pelvic fracture, and amputation proximal to the wrist or ankle. Age and a ground-level fall are special-patient criteria, and an isolated forearm fracture meets nothing.

quiz.q: A 32-week pregnant woman was in a crash and is supine on the stretcher with a blood pressure of 86/50. What should you do first?
choices: Sit her fully upright to relieve pressure on the diaphragm
Tilt her 15 to 30 degrees to the left or wedge the board
Deliver oxygen by nasal cannula and recheck in 10 minutes
Place her prone to protect the abdomen
quiz.why: After about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the vena cava when the patient is flat, cutting venous return and dropping the pressure. Left tilt relieves it immediately. Sitting up worsens brain perfusion, prone is unusable in trauma, and a cannula does not fix a mechanical obstruction.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: single vehicle into a guardrail, arterial bleeding
scenarios.intro:
It is 2140 on a two-lane road. Dispatch reports a single car into a guardrail with one occupant and "a lot of blood." State police are on scene with the roadway blocked and traffic stopped in both directions. Your ALS chase unit is 12 minutes out. The nearest hospital is a community ED 6 minutes away; the level I trauma center is 18 minutes away.

The car is upright, front end crushed inward, driver's door open. A trooper is holding a jacket against the driver's left thigh and the jacket is soaked through.

steps.prompt: The driver is a man in his thirties, awake, gripping the steering wheel and repeating that he is fine. There is a starred windshield and about `10 in` of intrusion at the driver's door. Bright red blood is pulsing out around the trooper's jacket every second or so. What do you do first?

choices.text: Take over the bleeding control immediately and expose the thigh
choices.feedback: Correct. Exsanguinating hemorrhage comes before airway in a patient who is talking to you. X-A-B-C. You cannot manage what you cannot see, so the pant leg comes off or gets cut away.

choices.text: Apply a cervical collar and begin manual in-line stabilization
choices.feedback: The mechanism justifies spinal concern, but a pulsing arterial bleed empties the patient in minutes. The collar can wait ninety seconds; the femoral artery cannot.

choices.text: Get a full set of vitals and a SAMPLE history before touching the wound
choices.feedback: Numbers do not stop bleeding. Gather history while your hands are already on the wound, not instead of it.

choices.text: Ask the trooper to keep holding pressure while you bring the stretcher over
choices.feedback: Acceptable only if a second provider is simultaneously taking over the wound. A jacket already soaked through is not controlling anything, so someone has to look at it now.

steps.prompt: You cut the pant leg away. There is a `4 in` gash on the medial thigh with bright red blood spurting in time with his pulse. The trooper's jacket is saturated and there is a wide pool on the floorboard. What is your action?

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops, and note the time
choices.feedback: Correct. A spurting arterial bleed in a limb is a tourniquet from the start; you do not climb the ladder step by step when the patient is visibly emptying. Tighten until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone, and write the time.

choices.text: Hold firm direct pressure for 3 minutes and reassess
choices.feedback: Reasonable for most bleeding, and it is never wrong to have a hand on the wound. But an arterial thigh wound with an established pool has already declared itself, and three minutes of watching is three minutes of loss.

choices.text: Elevate the leg and apply pressure over the femoral artery in the groin
choices.feedback: Elevation and pressure points were removed from bleeding control because they delay the interventions that work and have never been shown to help.

choices.text: Apply a pressure dressing and load for transport
choices.feedback: A pressure dressing holds control that already exists; it does not create it. Wrapping an uncontrolled arterial bleed just hides it under gauze while it continues.

steps.prompt: The tourniquet is on at `2145` and the spurting has slowed to a steady ooze, but it has not stopped. The thigh is thick and muscular. He is now quieter and looks gray.

choices.text: Place a second tourniquet directly above the first and tighten it
choices.feedback: Correct. A heavy thigh often needs two tourniquets to compress the femoral artery against the femur. Tighten the second until the ooze stops, and note that time too.

choices.text: Loosen the first tourniquet and reposition it higher
choices.feedback: Never loosen a tourniquet in the field. Releasing it restarts the bleeding and washes out the clot you just bought. Add, do not move.

choices.text: Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze under the tourniquet
choices.feedback: Packing is the answer for junctional wounds you cannot tourniquet. Here you have a working tool that is simply not tight enough, so tighten or add before switching techniques.

choices.text: Assume the ooze is venous and move on to the rest of the assessment
choices.feedback: Continued bleeding through a tourniquet means it is not occluding arterial inflow, and blood is still leaving. This is how patients arrive with a tourniquet on and no pressure.

steps.prompt: The second tourniquet stops the bleeding. He is on the stretcher, pale, cool, and clammy, answering questions slowly. The patient compartment is cold and his shirt is soaked with blood. What is your package?

choices.text: Oxygen to keep SpO2 at 94 percent or better, cut away wet clothing, blankets on, heat the compartment, supine
choices.feedback: Correct. You have done the treatment that matters, which was stopping the bleeding. Now protect the clot: cold blood does not clot, and hypothermia is the one leg of the lethal triad you control.

choices.text: Raise his legs 12 inches in shock position and cover with a sheet
choices.feedback: Shock position has no proven benefit in trauma and is no longer recommended. A single sheet over wet bloody clothing will not keep a shocky patient warm.

choices.text: Give him water since he is asking for a drink
choices.feedback: He is thirsty because he is in shock, and he is very likely headed for an operating room. Nothing by mouth.

choices.text: Oxygen and blankets, but leave the bloody clothing in place to avoid moving him
choices.feedback: Partly right. Oxygen and blankets are correct, but wet clothing wicks heat away faster than blankets replace it, so it has to come off.

steps.prompt: You are ready to move. Total scene time so far is `9 minutes`. The community ED is `6 minutes` away; the level I trauma center is `18 minutes` away. ALS is still `5 minutes` out. Where do you go?

choices.text: Level I trauma center, meeting ALS en route if the rendezvous does not delay you
choices.feedback: Correct. He meets physiologic criteria with a systolic under 90, so he goes to the highest level of trauma care available. He needs blood and a surgeon, and the extra 12 minutes buys both.

choices.text: Community ED because it is closest and he is unstable
choices.feedback: Understandable instinct, but a community ED will stabilize briefly and then transfer, and the transfer costs far more than 12 minutes. Field triage criteria exist precisely to prevent this detour.

choices.text: Wait on scene for ALS so he can get an IV before moving
choices.feedback: Nothing ALS carries fixes this. He needs blood products and an operating room, and waiting adds to a scene time already past the platinum ten.

choices.text: Request a helicopter to the scene
choices.feedback: With an 18-minute ground transport, the helicopter cannot be dispatched, land, package, and fly faster than you can drive. Air medical earns its place with long transports or inaccessible scenes.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **bleeding first, everything else second**. A spurting limb wound goes straight to a tourniquet rather than up the ladder one rung at a time, and a thick thigh commonly needs two. Once the tourniquet is on, it does not come off in the field and the time is written down.

Notice what the vitals did. His pressure was `92/78` while he was still compensating — a narrow pulse pressure with a heart rate of 136 is the tank draining, not a normal blood pressure. By the time the systolic read `86`, roughly a third of his volume was gone.

After the bleeding stops, the treatment is warmth, oxygen, supine, and a trauma center. Hypothermia is the leg of the lethal triad you own.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: fall from a ladder, head injury
scenarios.intro:
You are called to a home at 1510 for a man who fell while cleaning a gutter. His wife says the ladder slid out and he landed on the concrete driveway. She thinks the ladder was at the second-story gutter line, around `18 ft`. She heard him hit and came out to find him on his side.

Scene is safe, the ladder is down, and there is no blood pooling. The level II trauma center is `14 minutes` away; the local community hospital is `5 minutes`.

steps.prompt: He is a `58`-year-old man lying on his right side. His eyes are closed. When you say his name loudly, he opens his eyes and says "what... what happened... what happened" and repeats it. He squeezes your hand when asked. There is a lump over his left temple. His wife says he takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation.

choices.text: Score his GCS, protect the airway, and begin manual in-line stabilization
choices.feedback: Correct. GCS is your trend line, the airway is the treatment, and an 18-foot fall onto concrete plus repetitive questioning makes this a spine and brain patient from the first minute.

choices.text: Sit him up to help his breathing and get a history from him
choices.feedback: Sitting him up moves an unprotected spine after an 18-foot fall, and a man who cannot stop asking what happened cannot give you a history.

choices.text: Note that he is awake and talking, and focus on the lump over his temple
choices.feedback: Awake and talking is not the same as intact. Repetitive questioning is a real neurologic finding, and a temporal lump over an anticoagulated patient is the setup for an epidural bleed.

choices.text: Have the wife help you walk him to the stretcher since he can follow commands
choices.feedback: He meets none of the selective clearance criteria. He is not oriented, the mechanism is significant, and walking him risks moving an unstable spine.

steps.prompt: Score him. He opens his eyes when you call his name. He speaks in full sentences but cannot tell you the year or where he is, and keeps repeating the same question. He squeezes both of your hands on command. What is his GCS?

choices.text: E3, V4, M6 for a total of 13
choices.feedback: Correct. Eyes to speech is 3, confused conversation is 4, and obeying commands is 6. Thirteen is your baseline number, and the number that matters is whether it moves.

choices.text: E4, V4, M6 for a total of 14
choices.feedback: Close, but he did not open his eyes until you spoke. Spontaneous eye opening is 4; opening to speech is 3.

choices.text: E3, V3, M6 for a total of 12
choices.feedback: Inappropriate words, V3, means isolated words that do not form conversation. He speaks in full sentences that are simply wrong, which is confused conversation, V4.

choices.text: E3, V5, M6 for a total of 14
choices.feedback: V5 requires being oriented. He does not know the year or where he is, so he cannot score 5.

steps.prompt: You need to move him. He has no midline spinal tenderness that you can elicit, but he is not oriented, cannot reliably answer, and has an obviously deforming left wrist injury that he winces at. What is the spinal plan?

choices.text: Skip restriction, since he has no midline tenderness
choices.feedback: Selective clearance requires every criterion to be met. He fails on mental status, fails on reliability, and fails on a distracting injury, so the absence of tenderness proves nothing.

choices.text: Properly sized collar, log roll onto a scoop stretcher, then secure to the cot with torso first and head last
choices.feedback: Correct. He fails selective clearance three ways. A scoop or vacuum mattress restricts motion without the pressure injury and breathing restriction of a rigid board, and torso-first strapping keeps the head from levering.

choices.text: Collar plus full rigid long board with head blocks for the entire transport
choices.feedback: Restriction is right, but a rigid board for a 14-minute transport adds pain and pressure injury with no benefit. Use the board to move him, then get him onto padding.

choices.text: Collar only, and let him find a position of comfort on the cot
choices.feedback: A collar alone does not restrict the thoracic or lumbar spine, and a confused patient will move. He needs a device that moves him as one unit.

steps.prompt: Five minutes into transport he vomits without warning. He is secured to a scoop on the cot. What is your immediate action?

choices.text: Turn the entire secured device on its side as a unit and suction
choices.feedback: Correct. This is exactly why you strap so the whole assembly can be tipped. Vomiting even once after a head injury is a red flag, and his blood pressure is climbing while his pulse falls.

choices.text: Loosen the straps and roll him onto his side by hand
choices.feedback: Unstrapping mid-emesis costs you seconds you do not have and moves his spine in an uncontrolled way. The device turns as one piece for this exact reason.

choices.text: Suction the mouth while leaving him flat
choices.feedback: Suction is right and you should be doing it, but leaving a vomiting patient flat lets the rest run down the trachea. Tip the device first, then suction.

choices.text: Note the vomiting as a minor finding and continue to the community hospital
choices.feedback: A single episode of vomiting after head trauma is a rising-pressure sign, not a minor finding, and his vitals are trending toward Cushing's triad.

steps.prompt: Two minutes later his right pupil is `6 mm` and non-reactive, the left is `3 mm` and reactive, and his arms extend stiffly when you pinch his shoulder. He is no longer opening his eyes.

choices.text: Begin bag-valve-mask ventilation at 20 breaths per minute with high-flow oxygen
choices.feedback: Correct. A blown pupil, extensor posturing, a falling GCS, and Cushing's triad are active herniation. This is the one indication for controlled hyperventilation at 20 per minute, and you stop when the signs resolve.

choices.text: Ventilate at 10 to 12 per minute with high-flow oxygen
choices.feedback: That is the correct default for a head injury, and it is far better than nothing, but active herniation is the exception where 20 per minute is indicated.

choices.text: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 lpm and monitor
choices.feedback: He is breathing 8 times a minute. A mask cannot move air for a patient who is not moving enough himself, and his carbon dioxide is climbing, which swells the brain further.

choices.text: Hyperventilate at 30 breaths per minute to drop the pressure as fast as possible
choices.feedback: Too far. Driving carbon dioxide that low clamps cerebral vessels shut and starves the brain of the blood it is already short on. Twenty is the number.

steps.prompt: You are `9 minutes` from the level II trauma center and `3 minutes` from the community hospital, which has a CT scanner but no neurosurgery. He is anticoagulated on apixaban. Where do you go and what do you call in?

choices.text: Community hospital, because 3 minutes beats 9 minutes with a herniating patient
choices.feedback: A scan without a neurosurgeon only documents the bleed. He needs an operating room, and the transfer out will cost far more than the 6 minutes you saved.

choices.text: Level II trauma center with an early alert naming herniation signs and the anticoagulant
choices.feedback: Correct. He needs neurosurgery and reversal of his apixaban, and naming both on the radio gets the team and the reversal agent moving before you arrive.

choices.text: Level II trauma center, with a standard report given on arrival
choices.feedback: Right destination, wasted notice. An early alert is the whole reason a trauma team is standing in the bay when the doors open.

choices.text: Divert to a landing zone and request a helicopter to a level I center
choices.feedback: Setting up a landing zone for a patient who is 9 minutes from definitive care adds time he does not have. Air medical is for distance and inaccessibility, not for upgrading a nearby destination.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **the head injury that kills declares itself over minutes, and the number that matters is the trend**. He started at `GCS 13` with repetitive questioning, moved to `12` with a single episode of vomiting, then to `5` with a blown pupil and posturing. No single snapshot was the finding; the slope was.

Cushing's triad appeared right on schedule — pressure climbing from `148` to `212`, pulse falling from `92` to `46`, and respirations becoming slow and irregular. That combination plus a dilated pupil is the only time you ventilate at `20/min`, and you stop when it resolves.

Two details do heavy work here. He failed selective spinal clearance three separate ways, so the absence of midline tenderness meant nothing. And apixaban turns a modest bleed into a large one, which is why the anticoagulant belongs in your radio report, not just your chart.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: house fire, one patient out
scenarios.intro:
A working structure fire at 0340. Fire crews pulled an adult man out of a first-floor bedroom and walked him to you. The house is still burning and the scene is loud. Command says he was in the room roughly `6 minutes` before they reached him, and that the room was filled with smoke floor to ceiling.

He is standing next to your rig in what is left of a t-shirt and shorts. The nearest ED is `8 minutes` away. The regional burn center is `34 minutes` by ground.

steps.prompt: He is about `40`, coughing, and says "I'm okay, just get me some water." His shirt is partly melted onto his chest. His right arm is red and blistered from shoulder to fingertips. The front of his chest and abdomen are blistered and weeping. His face is sooty and there is black material around both nostrils. He is still wearing a wedding band and a watch. What do you do first?

choices.text: Stop the burning process, remove the watch and ring, and get him into the ambulance away from the heat
choices.feedback: Correct. Stopping the burn and removing constricting jewelry before swelling starts are both time-limited actions. In ten minutes that ring will not come off and the finger underneath will be at risk.

choices.text: Give him the water he is asking for while you assess
choices.feedback: Nothing by mouth. A burn this size is likely to need procedures and possibly an airway, and burn patients vomit readily.

choices.text: Peel the melted shirt fabric off his chest so you can see the burn
choices.feedback: Fabric stuck to skin is left alone and cut around. Pulling it off takes viable tissue with it and starts new bleeding.

choices.text: Apply cool wet sheets to the entire burned area to stop the pain
choices.feedback: Cooling is appropriate only for small burns, under about 10 percent, and only for 1 to 2 minutes. Wet sheets over a large burn drop the core temperature and worsen shock.

steps.prompt: In the ambulance you finish exposing him. The blistering covers the entire front of his chest and abdomen and the entire right arm circumferentially. His back, legs, and left arm are unburned. His face is sooty but the skin is only pink, without blisters. Using the rule of nines, what is his burn surface area?

choices.text: About 18 percent
choices.feedback: That counts only the front torso. The entire right arm adds another 9 percent.

choices.text: About 27 percent
choices.feedback: Correct. Front of torso is 18 percent and a whole arm is 9 percent, for 27 percent. The reddened face is superficial, and superficial burns are not counted in surface area.

choices.text: About 36 percent
choices.feedback: That counts the entire torso front and back. His back is unburned, so only the anterior 18 percent counts.

choices.text: About 31 percent, including the reddened face
choices.feedback: Superficial burns, the red painful ones with no blisters, are excluded from the surface area estimate. Only partial and full thickness count.

steps.prompt: Name what makes this a critical burn. He now has a hoarse voice, is coughing up gray-black sputum, and his `SpO2` reads `99%` on room air. Your partner says his oxygenation looks fine.

choices.text: It is not yet critical since the burns are partial thickness and under 30 percent
choices.feedback: Several criteria are already met independent of depth or size: a circumferential arm, suspected inhalation injury, and a fire in an enclosed space.

choices.text: Critical: suspected inhalation injury, circumferential arm burn, and 27 percent partial thickness in an enclosed-space fire
choices.feedback: Correct. Any one of those alone makes it critical. Soot at the nostrils, hoarseness, and carbonaceous sputum are the inhalation triad, and a circumferential burn will act as a tourniquet as it swells.

choices.text: Critical only because of the total surface area
choices.feedback: Partially right, but surface area is the least urgent of the three criteria he meets. The airway is what will kill him in the next hour.

choices.text: The 99 percent saturation is reassuring, so treat the burns and reassess
choices.feedback: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin 200 to 250 times more tightly than oxygen, and the pulse oximeter reads it as though it were oxygen. In a house fire, a perfect saturation is a trap.

steps.prompt: What oxygen and airway plan do you commit to for the ride?

choices.text: Non-rebreather at 15 lpm, sit him up, keep suction and a BVM at hand, and monitor his voice
choices.feedback: Correct. High-flow oxygen shortens carbon monoxide's half-life from hours to well under an hour. Sitting up slows swelling, and a changing voice is your earliest warning that the airway is closing.

choices.text: Nasal cannula at 4 lpm since his saturation is already 99 percent
choices.feedback: The saturation is meaningless here, and low-flow oxygen does almost nothing for carbon monoxide. He needs the highest concentration you can deliver.

choices.text: No oxygen, but reassess the airway every 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Withholding oxygen from a fire victim on the strength of a pulse oximeter reading is the single most common error in this call.

choices.text: Non-rebreather at 15 lpm with the patient lying flat
choices.feedback: Oxygen is right. Lying flat worsens facial and airway swelling, so keep him upright unless something else forces him down.

steps.prompt: The burns need to be covered. The patient is shivering and the compartment is cold. He asks for something on his chest because it is burning.

choices.text: Dry sterile dressings, gauze between the burned fingers, blankets over the top, and heat the compartment
choices.feedback: Correct. Burned skin has lost its ability to hold heat in, and his temperature is already `35.8 C`. Dry sterile covering plus aggressive warming is the whole plan.

choices.text: Burn gel dressings over the chest and arm to cool and soothe
choices.feedback: Gel dressings on 27 percent of a body will drive the core temperature down further in a patient who is already at 35.8 degrees. They are for small burns.

choices.text: Ice packs wrapped in towels over the worst blistering
choices.feedback: Never ice. It causes additional tissue injury at the burn margin and accelerates the hypothermia that is already developing.

choices.text: Dry sterile dressings and a single blanket, with the compartment left as is
choices.feedback: The dressings are right. One blanket in a cold compartment will not reverse a falling core temperature in a patient who has lost a quarter of his skin.

steps.prompt: Time to choose a destination. The nearest ED is `8 minutes` away and has no burn unit. The regional burn center is `34 minutes` by ground and has a helipad; a helicopter could reach you in `12 minutes` and fly him in `10`. His voice is getting hoarser.

choices.text: Ground to the nearest ED for immediate airway management, with an early burn alert and transfer arrangements
choices.feedback: Correct for this patient. A threatened airway beats burn-specific care in priority, and 8 minutes to a team that can secure an airway is the safest path. Burn transfer happens after the airway is protected.

choices.text: Ground directly to the burn center, 34 minutes away
choices.feedback: Correct destination for the burns, wrong call for this airway. A hoarsening voice means 34 minutes is a long time to gamble without the ability to intubate.

choices.text: Stage on scene and wait 12 minutes for the helicopter
choices.feedback: Twenty-two minutes of waiting and loading, with a closing airway, in exchange for a destination you could reach by ground. Air medical does not fix an airway on the ground.

choices.text: Nearest ED, with report given on arrival
choices.feedback: Right destination, no warning. Call ahead naming inhalation injury and 27 percent burns so the airway equipment and the burn transfer are being arranged while you drive.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: **in a fire victim, the airway outranks the burn**. The skin injury is what you can see and it is not what kills him tonight. Soot at the nostrils, a hoarse voice, and carbonaceous sputum after six minutes in a smoke-filled room predict an airway that swells shut over `30–60 minutes`.

The `SpO2` of `99%` was the deliberate trap. Carbon monoxide occupies hemoglobin and the pulse oximeter counts it as oxygen, so the number is meaningless in exactly the patients who need oxygen most. High-flow oxygen by non-rebreather, every time, on the story rather than the number.

On the arithmetic: anterior torso `18%` plus a whole arm `9%` equals `27%`, and the reddened face was superficial and therefore not counted. He met critical burn criteria three different ways — inhalation injury, a circumferential extremity burn, and surface area — and any single one of them would have been enough.

Last, the two time-limited actions you can only do early: get the ring and watch off before the swelling, and start fighting hypothermia before the core temperature falls. Burned skin cannot hold heat, and a cold burn patient bleeds, clots, and heals worse.
